title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: E<sub>a</sub> is measured from the reactants up to the top of the hill; ΔH is products minus reactants. Are the products above or below the reactants?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Which of the four rate factors in 13.1 changes when you chew a tablet? Think about how much of the solid can touch the acid at once.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: An effective collision needs the right orientation and enough energy. Besides colliding more often, what else changes about the collisions at a higher temperature?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Bacterial growth runs on enzyme-catalyzed reactions. Apply both effects of temperature: how often molecules collide, and how many collisions reach at least E<sub>a</sub>.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: The battery runs on chemical reactions. Ask what cold does to how often particles collide and to the fraction of collisions with at least E<sub>a</sub>, then what warming does.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: The forward reaction reads left to right; the reverse is the same equation read right to left, with the same coefficients and phases.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Equilibrium is defined by rates, not by amounts. Remember: equal rates, constant amounts.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Equilibrium is dynamic. Once the color is steady, have the two reactions stopped, or are they running at the same rate?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: The levels stop changing only when each trip forward is matched by a trip back. Then ask which tub the bigger beaker favors, and what the beakers and the tubs each stand for.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Products over reactants, with each coefficient as an exponent. All three species are gases, so all of them appear.
why: Products go on top and reactants on the bottom, each raised to its coefficient: 2 for SO<sub>3</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub>, 1 (not written) for O<sub>2</sub>; all three are gases, so none is left out.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Circle the phase labels first and cross out every (s) and (l). Then write products over reactants. Is the water here a liquid or a gas?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Plug the equilibrium concentrations into the expression from Exercise 1, squaring the terms with a coefficient of 2. Then compare K with 1.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Write K as products over reactants (every coefficient is 1), plug in the concentrations, and compare the result with 1.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Write K = [N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>] / [NO<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2</sup>, then plug in; don't forget to square [NO<sub>2</sub>].

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{6}\)
hint: Writing a reaction backward flips the expression, so K<sub>reverse</sub> = 1/K. Then ask which gas each K favors.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: (a)(b) Add → Away, Take → Toward. (c) ΔH is negative, so write heat as a product. (d) Count moles of gas on each side; a larger volume favors the side with more.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Add → Away, Take → Toward. Then follow the shift: does the amount of red FeSCN<sup>2+</sup> go up or down?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Slow breathing means CO<sub>2</sub> is not exhaled, so it builds up. Which way does adding CO<sub>2</sub> push the equilibrium, and what happens to [H<sup>+</sup>]?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Acid from plaque bacteria removes OH<sup>−</sup> from the enamel equilibrium. Take → Toward: which way does that shift it, and how long does each sip keep the stress on?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Only one kind of stress changes the value of K. Which of the four changes is it?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{6}\)
hint: A bigger volume means lower pressure. Count moles of gas on each side, and shift toward the side with more.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{7}\)
hint: (a) Write how KSCN splits into ions. (b) Which ion is already in the equilibrium? Add → Away. (c) Follow the shift to the red FeSCN<sup>2+</sup>.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{8}\)
hint: (a) Is heat written on the reactant or the product side? (b) Cooling removes heat: Take → Toward. (c) Do pure solids appear in K?

title: Problem 13.1
hint: Recall what collision theory says an effective collision needs. Which choice states that, and which choices contradict how gas particles and equilibrium behave?

title: Problem 13.2
hint: E<sub>a</sub> = top of hill − reactants; ΔH = products − reactants. For (d), a catalyst lowers only the hill, not the starting or ending energies.

title: Problem 13.3
hint: Activation energy is always measured from the reactants up to the top of the hill, not from zero and not from the products.

title: Problem 13.4
hint: (a) Compare each row with the one before. (b) Divide each value by the one above it. (c) Divide the 35 °C value by the 5 °C value. (d) Apply the same factor once more.

title: Problem 13.5
hint: Go through the rate factors: temperature, concentration, and surface area. For each choice, does the change speed the reaction up or slow it down?

title: Problem 13.6
hint: (a) Apply both effects of a higher temperature on collisions. (b) Enzymes are proteins that need their exact shape. (c) Think of the balance between faster collisions and losing that shape.

title: Problem 13.7
hint: (a) Count the 10 °C steps between the two temperatures, and double once per step. (b) Compare with 4 to 60 °C. (c) Does cold kill bacteria, or slow their reactions?

title: Problem 13.8
hint: Grinding is a physical change. Which rate factor changes when a solid becomes a fine dust?

title: Problem 13.9
hint: Burning is fuel reacting with O<sub>2</sub>. Which rate factor changes in oxygen-enriched air, and what does that do to the number of collisions per second?

title: Problem 13.10
hint: (a) Apply both effects of a higher temperature on collisions. (b) What is the only thing that changes the height of the hill?

title: Problem 13.11
hint: Is equilibrium defined by amounts or by rates? Do the reactions stop, and does “constant” mean the same as “equal”?

title: Problem 13.12
hint: The pressure stopped changing, so the bottle is at equilibrium. What is still happening at the molecular level at equilibrium? Does constant mean equal?

title: Problem 13.13
hint: (a) Read the equation each way. (b) With only C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, which direction has nothing to collide? (c) How do the rates change as substances build up or get used? (d) Is anything used up completely?

title: Problem 13.14
hint: With only reactants at the start, the reverse reaction has no products to collide. How does its rate change as products build up, and where does it end?

title: Problem 13.15
hint: (a) Each flask can run only the direction its starting gases allow. (b) Equilibrium contains everything in the equation. (c) Compare the atoms in each flask; equilibrium can be reached from either side.

title: Problem 13.16
hint: Equilibrium needs the reverse process, condensation, to keep pace with evaporation. In which container can the vapor collect above the liquid?

title: Problem 13.17
hint: Equal rates, constant amounts. Does a steady color mean the reactions stopped? And does constant mean equal?

title: Problem 13.18
hint: Products over reactants, with each coefficient as an exponent (not a multiplier).

title: Problem 13.19
hint: Circle the phase labels and cross out (s) and (l). Then write products over reactants with exponents. Is the water here a liquid or a gas?

title: Problem 13.20
hint: For each: cross out every (s) and (l), then write products over reactants with coefficients as exponents. If nothing is left on the bottom, the expression has no denominator.

title: Problem 13.21
hint: The species on top are the products and those on the bottom are the reactants; the exponents are the coefficients. Check that the equation balances.

title: Problem 13.22
hint: Write K (every coefficient is 1): multiply the products on top, multiply the reactants on the bottom, then divide.

title: Problem 13.23
hint: (a) Products over reactants, with coefficients as exponents. (b) Square both [H<sub>2</sub>] and [H<sub>2</sub>S]. (c) Compare K with 1.

title: Problem 13.24
hint: Leave the solid out. What is left is just the two gas concentrations, multiplied together.

title: Problem 13.25
hint: (a) Product over reactants; NO has a coefficient of 2. (b) Plug in each row, squaring [NO]. (c) Compare the three results. (d) Compare K with 1.

title: Problem 13.26
hint: What question does K answer, and what question does rate answer (Section 13.1)? Which one explains why nothing happens until a spark?

title: Problem 13.27
hint: (a) K<sub>reverse</sub> = 1/K. (b) Does writing the reaction backward change what is in the flask? (c) Compare each K with 1: very large, very small, or close to 1 (about 0.1–10)?

title: Problem 13.28
hint: Is Br<sub>2</sub> a reactant or a product, and which way does adding it push the system? Did this stress change the temperature?

title: Problem 13.29
hint: Find the direction first with Add → Away, Take → Toward. Then everything on the side the system shifts toward goes up, and everything on the other side goes down.

title: Problem 13.30
hint: (a)(b) Add → Away, Take → Toward for Cl<sup>−</sup>. (c)(d) ΔH is positive, so write heat as a reactant. Pink is on the left, blue on the right. (e) Only one kind of stress changes K.

title: Problem 13.31
hint: The muscle removes O<sub>2</sub>. Take → Toward: which side of the equation is O<sub>2</sub> on?

title: Problem 13.32
hint: (a) Less O<sub>2</sub> acts like removing a reactant: Take → Toward. (b) More Hb is adding a reactant. (c) What is the only stress that changes K?

title: Problem 13.33
hint: O<sub>2</sub> is a reactant in this equilibrium. Add → Away: which way does adding a lot of it push the system? Remember that only temperature changes K.

title: Problem 13.34
hint: Fast breathing removes CO<sub>2</sub>. Use Take → Toward, then follow [H<sup>+</sup>]: does less H<sup>+</sup> mean a higher or a lower pH?

title: Problem 13.35
hint: H<sup>+</sup> is not in the equation, but it reacts with OH<sup>−</sup>, which is. Is OH<sup>−</sup> being added or taken away?

title: Problem 13.36
hint: (a) Ca<sup>2+</sup> and phosphate are products: Add → Away. (b) Which is the weaker base, F<sup>−</sup> or OH<sup>−</sup>, and so harder for H<sup>+</sup> to remove? (c) Less saliva: fewer ions added, less acid neutralized.

title: Problem 13.37
hint: When ΔH is negative, is heat a reactant or a product? Which way does adding heat push the system? Which kind of stress is the one that changes K?

title: Problem 13.38
hint: Heating made more brown NO<sub>2</sub>, so heating shifted the system right. With Add → Away, which side must heat be on? Then, more product means what for K?

title: Problem 13.39
hint: (a) K grew as the temperature rose; Add → Away tells you which side heat is on. (b) Write heat on that side. (c) Add heat. (d) Does a catalyst speed one direction or both?

title: Problem 13.40
hint: Heat is a product here. Which way does adding heat push the system? Which kind of stress is the one that changes K?

title: Problem 13.41
hint: Count moles of gas on each side. Does a smaller volume (higher pressure) favor the side with more or fewer moles of gas?

title: Problem 13.42
hint: A larger volume shifts toward the side with more moles of gas. Count gases only; solids are not counted.

title: Problem 13.43
hint: Argon is not in the equation, and the volume is fixed. Did the concentration (mol/L) of N<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>, or NH<sub>3</sub> change?

title: Problem 13.44
hint: A catalyst lowers the hill for both the forward and the reverse reactions. Does it change how fast equilibrium is reached, where it ends up, or both?

title: Problem 13.45
hint: Use Add → Away, Take → Toward; write heat as a reactant (ΔH positive); count gas moles for volume. Then follow H<sub>2</sub>O, a reactant. Only temperature changes K.

title: Problem 13.46
hint: Does a pure solid appear in the K expression? If adding the solid changed [OH<sup>−</sup>], what would that do to the value of the expression?

title: Problem 13.47
hint: (a) Opening the can removes CO<sub>2</sub>(g): Take → Toward. (b) Heat is a product; warming adds heat. (c) Is an open can a closed system?

title: Problem 13.48
hint: (a) Each mole of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> lost makes 2 mol NO<sub>2</sub>. (b) Are the concentrations still changing? (c) Square [NO<sub>2</sub>] in K. (d) ΔH is positive: does heating make K larger or smaller?

title: Problem 13.49
hint: (a) Compare with the normal ranges. (b) Fast breathing removes CO<sub>2</sub>: Take → Toward. (c) CO<sub>2</sub> building up is adding: Add → Away. (d) Catalysts speed both directions. (e) Leave out water; only temperature changes K.

title: Problem 13.50
hint: (a) Square [NH<sub>3</sub>] and cube [H<sub>2</sub>]. (b) ΔH is negative, so heat is a product. (c) Separate rate (Section 13.1) from equilibrium. (d) Does a catalyst speed one direction or both?

title: Problem 13.51
hint: (a) Cross out the solids; the water here is a gas. (b) More water vapor is adding a reactant. (c) Heat is a product; warming adds it. (d) Do solids appear in K?

title: Problem 13.52
hint: (a) Products over reactants, with exponents. (b) Compare K with 1. (c) K tells how far, not how fast. (d) What does a catalyst do to E<sub>a</sub>? (e) ΔH is negative, so heat is a product.

title: Problem 13.53
hint: The levels stop changing when each forward trip is matched by a reverse trip: equal rates. Do equal rates mean equal amounts?

title: Problem 13.54
hint: (a) Flip the expression: the old reactants go on top, and coefficients stay as exponents. (b) K<sub>reverse</sub> = 1/K. (c) Compare each K with 1.

title: Problem 13.55
hint: Write the dissociation of KNO<sub>3</sub> first. Does either ion appear in the equilibrium?

title: Problem 13.56
hint: (a) Which side is heat written on? (b) Add → Away, Take → Toward; solids cause no shift; count only gas moles for volume; cooling removes heat. (c) Only temperature changes K.

title: Problem 13.57
hint: Doubling the volume lowers the pressure. Count moles of gas on each side: does lower pressure favor the side with more or fewer moles of gas?

title: Problem 13.58
hint: A larger volume shifts toward more moles of gas. Count only the gases on each side; a solid counts as zero.

title: Problem 13.59
hint: (a) Write the ions NaHCO<sub>3</sub> splits into. (b) Which ion is already in the equilibrium? Add → Away. (c) Follow the shift to H<sup>+</sup>, then to the pH.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Products over reactants, as for any K. Water is the solvent, a pure liquid, so cross it out.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Write the solid breaking into one Mg<sup>2+</sup> and two OH<sup>−</sup>; leave out the solid, and the 2 becomes an exponent. Then: OH<sup>−</sup> is a common ion, so Add → Away.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: (a) Lead(II) means Pb<sup>2+</sup>; crisscross the charges, then write the solid dissolving into its ions. (b) Compare K<sub>sp</sub> with 1.
